facts.statement: Dingavis was an extinct ornithuromorph dinosaur that lived in present-day China during the Early Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: Dingavis is an extinct genus of ornithuromorph dinosaurs from the Early Cretaceous of present-day China.

facts.statement: A fossil skeleton of Dingavis was excavated at the Sihedang site in Liaoning.
facts.quote: At Sihedang in Liaoning a fossil skeleton was excavated.

facts.statement: The fossil specimen, catalogued as IVPP V20284, was found in the Aptian-aged Yixian Formation.
facts.quote: Catalogued as IVPP V20284, it was found in a layer of the Yixian Formation dating from the Aptian.

facts.statement: The fossil preserves feather remains located at the neck.
facts.quote: It preserves feather remains at the neck.

facts.statement: Approximately forty gastroliths were preserved in the fossil specimen.
facts.quote: About forty gastroliths have been preserved.

facts.statement: The fossil specimen was acquired by the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology in Beijing.
facts.quote: The specimen was acquired by the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology in Beijing.

facts.statement: The generic name Dingavis combines the name of Ding Wenjiang, known as the "Father of Chinese Geology", with the Latin word for bird.
facts.quote: The generic name combines the name of Ding Wenjiang, the "Father of Chinese Geology", with a Latin avis, "bird".

facts.statement: The beak of the related genus Juehuaornis equals 63 to 65% of the total skull length.
facts.quote: Juehuaornis has a long beak which equals 63 to 65% of the total skull length.

facts.statement: The gastroliths found in the fossil are large, with a diameter ranging from 2 to 4 cm.
facts.quote: The gastroliths are large, with a diameter of 2 - 4 cm.

facts.statement: The related genus Juehuaornis was placed in the Ornithuromorpha clade in 2015.
facts.quote: Juehuaornis was placed in the Ornithuromorpha (redefined as a stem-based clade) in 2015.

facts.statement: In 2016, researchers suggested that Dingavis might be cogeneric with Changzuiornis and Juehuaornis, which would grant priority to Juehuaornis.
facts.quote: In 2016, it was suggested that Dingavis might be cogeneric to the closely related genera Changzuiornis and Juehuaornis that might have been found in the same formation, in which case Juehuaornis would have priority.

facts.statement: Dingavis lived during the Aptian stage, approximately between 121.4 and 113.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Aptian to Aptian (121.4 to 113.2 million years ago)

rejected.statement: The fossil consists of an almost complete and associated skeleton including the skull, preserved compressed on a plate.
rejected.quote: It consists of an almost complete and associated skeleton with skull, compressed on a plate.

rejected.statement: The type species Dingavis longimaxilla was named and described in 2015 by Jingmai O'Connor, Wang Min, and Hu Han.
rejected.quote: In 2015 the type species Dingavis longimaxilla was named and described by Jingmai O'Connor, Wang Min and Hu Han.
